source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Evidence that the antihypertensive dose is too low, because ankle edema generally indicates inadequate arteriolar vasodilation.","B":"Proof of new or worsening heart failure, because edema during dihydropyridine therapy always represents total-body fluid overload.","C":"An adverse effect unrelated to calcium-channel blockade, because this drug class does not meaningfully alter peripheral capillary pressure.","D":"A recognized dose-related effect of dihydropyridine therapy caused by arteriolar dilation and increased capillary hydrostatic pressure."}}
source_row.rationale: Peripheral edema is a common, dose-dependent adverse effect of dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, resulting from selective arteriolar vasodilation that increases capillary hydrostatic pressure, rather than true fluid overload or worsening heart failure. It should still be reported and evaluated, but is a recognized class effect rather than always indicating a more serious cardiac problem.
source_row.source_detail: DailyMed amlodipine labeling, Adverse Reactions: edema is the most common adverse reaction and is dose related. Label revised 2026-05; reviewed 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.
